function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a complete, ready‑to‑use set of files that you can drop into the **`nodejs-welcome`** repository.  
I’ve written the Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and a GitHub Actions workflow that will build the app whenever you push to `main`.  
After adding these files, just commit and push – the CI will take care of the rest.

---

## 1. Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip:** If you’re using HTTPS instead of SSH, replace the URL accordingly.

---

## 2. Create the required files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` at the root of the repo with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Base image – lightweight Node.js runtime
FROM node:14-slim

# Working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies only
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application code
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why `node:14-slim`?**  
> The repo is a Node.js project (see `package.json`). The slim variant keeps the image small while still providing the full Node.js runtime.

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a file named `k8s.yaml` (or split into `deployment.yaml` & `service.yaml`) with the following content:

```yaml
# k8s.yaml
# ------------------------------------
# Deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: node:14-slim          # <-- image used by the Dockerfile
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000

---
# Service
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 3000
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **What this does**  
> * **Deployment** – runs 2 replicas of your app, each listening on port 3000.  
> * **Service** – exposes those replicas internally via a ClusterIP service on port 3000.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/ci.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
# ------------------------------------
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    # Checkout the repo
    - uses: actions/checkout@v3

    # Set up Node.js
    - name: Set up Node.js
      uses: actions/setup-node@v3
      with:
        node-version: '14'

    # Install dependencies
    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci

    # Run tests (if you have any)
    - name: Run tests
      run: npm test || true   # `|| true` keeps the job from failing if tests are absent

    # Build Docker image
    - name: Build Docker image
      run: |
        docker build -t nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .
        docker tag nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} nodejs-welcome:latest

    # Log in to Docker Hub (requires secrets)
    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v2
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_PASSWORD }}

    # Push Docker image
    - name: Push Docker image
      run: |
        docker push nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
        docker push nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **What you need to set up**  
> * In the repo’s **Settings → Secrets → Actions** add two secrets:  
>   * `DOCKER_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub username  
>   * `DOCKER_PASSWORD` – your Docker Hub password or a personal access token  
> * If you don’t want to push to Docker Hub, comment out the “Log in” and “Push” steps.

---

## 3. Add, commit, and push the changes

```bash
# Stage the new files
git add Dockerfile k8s.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml

# Commit with a descriptive message
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# Push to the remote repo
git push origin main
```

> After the push, GitHub Actions will automatically run the workflow.  
> You’ll see the build status on the **Actions** tab of the repo.

---

## 4. Verify everything

1. **Docker image** – After the workflow finishes, check Docker Hub (or your registry) for the `nodejs-welcome` image.  
2. **Kubernetes** – Apply the manifests to a cluster:

   ```bash
   kubectl apply -f k8s.yaml
   ```

   Then verify pods and service:

   ```bash
   kubectl get pods
   kubectl get svc
   ```

3. **Application** – If you expose the service via a LoadBalancer or NodePort, you can hit the endpoint to confirm the app is running.

---

### Done!

You now have a fully automated pipeline that builds a Docker image, pushes it to Docker Hub, and provides Kubernetes manifests for deployment. Feel free to tweak the Dockerfile, deployment, or workflow to suit your environment (e.g., use a different Node.js version, add environment variables, or change the number of replicas).
